Among events already started, which event should be chosen first to avoid wasting a near deadline?
A min-heap can always give you the available event with the smallest end day.
When there are no active events, you do not need to inspect every empty day before the next start day.
title: Largest Number of Events That Can Be Attended

notes: Each event can be attended on any one integer day in its inclusive [startDay, endDay] range.
Attending one event uses that day, so at most one event may be attended on any day.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: Attend the first event on day 1, the second on day 2, and the third on day 3.
One valid schedule is to attend the two [1,2] events on days 1 and 2, then attend [2,3] on day 3 and [3,4] on day 4.

content.problemStatement:
You receive an array of `events` where `events[i] = [startDay_i, endDay_i]`. Every event `i` starts at `startDay_i`\_ and ends at `endDay_i`.

You can attend an event `i` at any day `d` where `startDay_i <= d <= endDay_i`. You can only attend one event at any time `d`.

Output *the largest number of events you can attend*.

**Example 1:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2020/02/05/e1.png)

```
Input: events = [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]]
Output: 3
Explanation: You can attend all the three events.
One way to attend them all is as shown.
Attend the first event on day 1.
Attend the second event on day 2.
Attend the third event on day 3.
```

**Example 2:**

```
Input: events= [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,2]]
Output: 4
```

**Constraints:**

* `1 <= events.length <= 10^5`
* `events[i].length == 2`
* `1 <= startDay_i <= endDay_i <= 10^5`

notes: The heap always contains events that have started but are not yet attended or expired.
When no event is currently available, the sweep jumps directly to the next event start day.
solution.approach: Sort events by start day. Sweep through calendar days, add every event that has started to a min-heap keyed by end day, discard expired events, and attend the available event with the earliest end day. Choosing the earliest-ending available event preserves future days for events with later deadlines.

better.complexity: O(n log n + D alpha(D)) time and O(D) auxiliary space for D <= 10^5.
better.description: Sort events by end day and, for each event, assign the earliest currently unused day at or after its start. An ordered free-day structure such as a disjoint-set "next free day" table can locate and consume that day efficiently.

optimal.complexity: O(n log n + D) time and O(n) space, where n is the number of events and D is the largest relevant day.
optimal.description: Sort events by start day and sweep day by day. Put all events that have started into a min-heap by end day, remove expired events, and attend the event with the smallest end day. This greedy invariant is optimal because delaying an earlier-deadline event can only reduce future feasibility.

bruteForce.complexity: Exponential time in the number of events; additional recursion/state space is also exponential in the worst case.
bruteForce.description: Try every possible choice of attending or skipping each event and assign a distinct valid day to attended events. This is exponential and is practical only for very small inputs.

solution.timeComplexity: O(n log n + D), where D is the largest day reached by the sweep and D <= 10^5.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the sorted events and min-heap.

followUps: Can you avoid scanning every day when the event ranges contain very large idle gaps?
What changes if each event requires two consecutive days instead of one?
What changes if you can attend up to k events on the same day?

learningObjectives: Recognize when an earliest-deadline greedy rule is appropriate for interval scheduling.
Use sorting to organize events by start time.
Use a min-heap (priority queue) to track the most urgent available event.
Design adversarial cases around deadlines, duplicates, overlaps, and boundary values.
